Twenty-two verses, Meccan

Then He followed this line of argument with another, namely His saying: ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind,﴾ (Al-Buruj 85:20), mentioning a third aspect, which is that this matter is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), unchangeable. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

and al-Dahhak. Several points support the soundness of this possibility:

The second: What Abu Hurayrah narrated, that he (ﷺ) said: "The angels come to the doors of the mosque and record the people. When the imam comes out, the scrolls are folded." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:78). It has been narrated: "The angels of the night and the day attend at the time of the Fajr prayer, so this prayer is called witnessed because of the witnessing of the angels." Likewise, Friday.

Third: "The witnessed" is interpreted as the Day of 'Arafah, and "the witness" is whoever attends it from the pilgrims. The oath by it is fitting to magnify the matter of the Hajj. It has been narrated that God says to the angels on the Day of 'Arafah: "Look at My servants, disheveled and dusty, who have come to Me from every deep mountain pass. I call you to witness that I have forgiven them." And Iblis cries out and puts dust on his head, because of what he sees of that. The evidence that the Day of 'Arafah is named "witnessed" is His saying: ﴿And upon every lean camel they come from every deep mountain pass, that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:27–28).

Fifth: The verse is interpreted as referring to the Day of Friday, the Day of 'Arafah, and the Day of Sacrifice all together, for they are great days, and God swore by them just as He swore by the ten nights, by the even and the odd. Perhaps the verse is general to every great day of the days of this world, and every noble station of its stations, and also to the Day of Resurrection, for it is a great day, as He said: ﴿For a great Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ (Al-Mutaffifin 83:5–6). And He said: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from the scene of a tremendous Day﴾ (Maryam 19:37). What supports the soundness of this interpretation is that the words "witness" and "witnessed" came in indefinite form, so it is possible that this means the intention was not directed to a specific day, and therefore it is not definite.

As for the first aspect, namely that "the witness" is understood as the one by whose word a claim is established, they have mentioned many aspects under this assumption.

First: The witness is God, exalted is He, based on His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:18), and His saying: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say, "Allah"﴾ (Al-An'am 6:19), and His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾ (Fussilat 41:53). And "the witnessed" is monotheism (tawhid), based on His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾, or prophethood: ﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you"﴾ (Al-An'am 6:19).

Second: The witness is Muhammad (ﷺ), and "the witnessed against" are all the prophets, based on His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:41), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:45).

Third: The witness is the prophets, and "the witnessed against" is the nations, based on His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:41).

Fourth: The witness is all possible and originated things (al-mumkinat wal-muhdathat), and "the witnessed against" is the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud). This is a possibility I mentioned myself, and I took it from the statement of the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun): "This is inference from the witness to the absent." Under this assumption, the oath is made by creation and the Creator, and by the making and the Maker.

Fifth: The witness is the angel, based on His saying: ﴿And there will come every soul, with it a driver and a witness﴾ (Qaf 50:21). And "the witnessed against" are the responsible persons (mukallafun).

Sixth: The witness is the angel, and "the witnessed against" is the human being against whom his limbs bear witness on the Day of Resurrection. He said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them﴾ (An-Nur 24:24), and ﴿They will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ (Fussilat 41:21). This is the view of 'Ata al-Khurasani.

As for the third aspect, these are views based on narrations, not on derivation (ishtiqaq).

The first of them: The witness is Friday, and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated that he (peace be upon him) said: "The promised Day is the Day of Resurrection, the witness is Friday, and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah. Friday is God's treasure for us." And from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: "The witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah, and the witness is Friday. No sun has risen or set upon a day more excellent than it. In it there is an hour in which no believing servant who calls upon God for good will coincide with it without being granted it, and who seeks refuge from evil without being protected from it." And from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, as a mursal report from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The lord of days is Friday, which is the witness, and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah." This is the view of many scholars, such as 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Qatadah said: "Witness and witnessed are two days which God magnified among the days of this world, as it is related that the witness is Friday and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah."

The second: The witness is the Day of 'Arafah, and the witnessed is the Day of Sacrifice, because they are two days which God magnified, and He made them among the days of the pillars of the days of the Hajj. These two days testify for whoever attends them with faith and deserving of mercy. Therefore, it is possible for this meaning that the Day of Sacrifice is a witness for whoever attends it in a similar way, based on this report.

The third: The witness is Jesus, based on His saying, quoted about him: ﴿And I was a witness over them﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:117).

The fourth: The witness is Allah, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers told the truth"﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:52), and His saying: ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾ (Al-Mujadilah 58:7).

The fifth: The witness is the human being, and the witnessed is monotheism, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He took from the children of Adam... and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:172).

The sixth: The witness is the human being, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. As for the human being being a witness, it is based on His saying: ﴿They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:172). And as for the Day of Resurrection being witnessed, it is based on His saying: ﴿Lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:172). These are the summarized aspects, and Allah knows best the true realities of the Qur'an.

This is His saying: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an,﴾ (Al-Buruj 85:21). This is the order of the surah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sky containing the constellations,﴾ ﴿and by the promised Day,﴾ ﴿and by the witness and the witnessed.﴾

Know that there are three opinions regarding "the constellations" (al-buruj):

First: They are the twelve constellations, which are well known. The oath by them is fitting because of the wondrous wisdom in them, for the sun's movement through them is connected to the interests of the lower world. Without doubt, the interests of the lower world are tied to the sun's movement, and this indicates that they have a wise Creator. Al-Jubba'i said: "This oath refers to the lowest heaven, since the constellations are in it." But know that this is an error, and its verification has been mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with the adornment of the stars﴾ (As-Saffat 37:6).

Second: The constellations are the stations of the moon (manazil al-qamar), and the oath by them is fitting because of the wondrous effects of the moon's movement and motion.

Third: The constellations are the great stars, called "buruj" because of their prominence (zuhur).

As for "the promised Day," it is the Day of Resurrection, as narrated by Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that the intended meaning of ﴿and the promised Day﴾ is because of the splitting of the sky, its annihilation, and the nullification of its constellations.

As for "the witness and the witnessed," the statements of the exegetes have varied greatly concerning it. Al-Qaffal was the best of people in speech about it. He said: The word "witness" (shahid) applies to two things:

One of them: the witness by whom claims and rights are established.

The second: the witness in the sense of "present" (hadir), as in His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ (Al-An'am 6:73). It is said: "So-and-so is a witness (shahid), and so-and-so is absent (ghaib)." Interpreting the verse according to this second possibility is more appropriate, for if the intended meaning were the first, the word "witnessed" (mashhud) would not be free of a particle of relation, so one would say "mashhud 'alayhi" (witnessed against) or "mashhud lahu" (witnessed for). This is the apparent meaning. However, it is also possible that "mashhud" means "mashhud 'alayhi," and the particle was omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the covenant was ever questioned﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:34), meaning "questioned about it." Having understood this introduction, we say: If we take "shuhud" as presence, the verse may bear several interpretations.

First: The "witnessed" is the Day of Resurrection, and the "witness" is the assembly in which they are present. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas

*[Page 105]*

and al-Dahhak. Several points support the soundness of this possibility:

The first: There is no presence greater than that presence, for God gathers in it the creation of the first and the last, of angels, prophets, jinn, and humans. And turning the word to its most complete referent is more appropriate.

The second: He mentioned the promised Day, which is the Day of Resurrection, and then mentioned immediately after it: "﴿and witness and witnessed﴾." This suits the interpretation that "the witness" is whoever is present among the creatures on that Day, and "the witnessed" is what occurs on that Day of wonders.

The third: God described the Day of Resurrection as "witnessed" in His saying: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from the scene of a tremendous Day﴾ (Maryam 19:37). He also said: ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a witnessed Day﴾ (Hud 11:103). He said: ﴿On the Day He calls you, and you will respond with His praise﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:52). And He said: ﴿It will be but one shout, and at once they will all be brought before Us﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:53). As for the indefinite form of the two words, it is either according to what we mentioned in explaining His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾ (At-Takwir 81:14), as if it were said: "and what its multitude has exceeded of witness and witnessed," or it is due to ambiguity in the description, as if it were said: "a witness and a witnessed whose description cannot be comprehended." The oath by the Day of Resurrection is fitting as an alert to God's power, since it is the Day of Judgment and recompense, and the Day on which God alone holds sovereignty and rule. This interpretation was chosen by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Hasan ibn Ali, Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, and al-Thawri.

Second: "The witnessed" is interpreted as the Day of Friday (Jumu'ah), and this is the view of Ibn Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr. This is because it is a day on which the Muslims attend for prayer and the remembrance of God. Two reports indicate that this day is named "the witnessed":

The first: What Abu al-Darda' narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Increase your prayers upon me on Friday, for it is a witnessed day, which the angels attend."

The second: What Abu Hurayrah narrated, that he (ﷺ) said: "The angels come to the doors of the mosque and record the people. When the imam comes out, the scrolls are folded." This special feature exists only on this day, so it is permissible to call it "witnessed" for this reason. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:78). It has been narrated: "The angels of the night and the day attend at the time of the Fajr prayer, so this prayer is called witnessed because of the witnessing of the angels." Likewise, Friday.

Third: "The witnessed" is interpreted as the Day of 'Arafah, and "the witness" is whoever attends it from the pilgrims. The oath by it is fitting to magnify the matter of the Hajj. It has been narrated that God says to the angels on the Day of 'Arafah: "Look at My servants, disheveled and dusty, who have come to Me from every deep mountain pass. I call you to witness that I have forgiven them." And Iblis cries out and puts dust on his head, because of what he sees of that. The evidence that the Day of 'Arafah is named "witnessed" is His saying: ﴿And upon every lean camel they come from every deep mountain pass, that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:27–28).

Fourth: "The witnessed" is the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), because it is the greatest gathering in this world, for the people of East and West gather on that day at Mina and Muzdalifah, and it is the festival of the Muslims. The purpose of the oath by it is to magnify the matter of the Hajj.

Fifth: The verse is interpreted as referring to the Day of Friday, the Day of 'Arafah, and the Day of Sacrifice all together, for they are great days, and God swore by them just as He swore by the ten nights, by the even and the odd. Perhaps the verse is general to every great day of the days of this world, and every noble station of its stations, and also to the Day of Resurrection, for it is a great day, as He said: ﴿For a great Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ (Al-Mutaffifin 83:5–6). And He said: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from the scene of a tremendous Day﴾ (Maryam 19:37). What supports the soundness of this interpretation is that the words "witness" and "witnessed" came in indefinite form, so it is possible that this means the intention was not directed to a specific day, and therefore it is not definite.

As for the first aspect, namely that "the witness" is understood as the one by whose word a claim is established, they have mentioned many aspects under this assumption.

First: The witness is God, exalted is He, based on His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:18), and His saying: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest as testimony?" Say, "Allah"﴾ (Al-An'am 6:19), and His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾ (Fussilat 41:53). And "the witnessed" is monotheism (tawhid), based on His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾, or prophethood: ﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you"﴾ (Al-An'am 6:19).

Second: The witness is Muhammad (ﷺ), and "the witnessed against" are all the prophets, based on His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:41), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:45).

Third: The witness is the prophets, and "the witnessed against" is the nations, based on His saying: ﴿So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:41).

Fourth: The witness is all possible and originated things (al-mumkinat wal-muhdathat), and "the witnessed against" is the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud). This is a possibility I mentioned myself, and I took it from the statement of the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun): "This is inference from the witness to the absent." Under this assumption, the oath is made by creation and the Creator, and by the making and the Maker.

Fifth: The witness is the angel, based on His saying: ﴿And there will come every soul, with it a driver and a witness﴾ (Qaf 50:21). And "the witnessed against" are the responsible persons (mukallafun).

Sixth: The witness is the angel, and "the witnessed against" is the human being against whom his limbs bear witness on the Day of Resurrection. He said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them﴾ (An-Nur 24:24), and ﴿They will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ (Fussilat 41:21). This is the view of 'Ata al-Khurasani.

As for the third aspect, these are views based on narrations, not on derivation (ishtiqaq).

The first of them: The witness is Friday, and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated that he (peace be upon him) said: "The promised Day is the Day of Resurrection, the witness is Friday, and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah. Friday is God's treasure for us." And from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: "The witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah, and the witness is Friday. No sun has risen or set upon a day more excellent than it. In it there is an hour in which no believing servant who calls upon God for good will coincide with it without being granted it, and who seeks refuge from evil without being protected from it." And from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, as a mursal report from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The lord of days is Friday, which is the witness, and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah." This is the view of many scholars, such as 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan al-Basri, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Qatadah said: "Witness and witnessed are two days which God magnified among the days of this world, as it is related that the witness is Friday and the witnessed is the Day of 'Arafah."

The second: The witness is the Day of 'Arafah, and the witnessed is the Day of Sacrifice, because they are two days which God magnified, and He made them among the days of the pillars of the days of the Hajj. These two days testify for whoever attends them with faith and deserving of mercy. It has been narrated that he (peace be upon him) sacrificed two rams, and said regarding one of them: "This is on behalf of whoever bears witness for me that I conveyed the message." Therefore, it is possible for this meaning that the Day of Sacrifice is a witness for whoever attends it in a similar way, based on this report.

The third: The witness is Jesus, based on His saying, quoted about him: ﴿And I was a witness over them﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:117).

The fourth: The witness is Allah, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers told the truth"﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:52), and His saying: ﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾ (Al-Mujadilah 58:7).

The fifth: The witness is the human being, and the witnessed is monotheism, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He took from the children of Adam... and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:172).

The sixth: The witness is the human being, and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. As for the human being being a witness, it is based on His saying: ﴿They said, "Yes, we testify"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:172). And as for the Day of Resurrection being witnessed, it is based on His saying: ﴿Lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:172). These are the summarized aspects, and Allah knows best the true realities of the Qur'an.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench, the fire fueled with wood, when they sat beside it, and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers.﴾

Know that the oath requires an answer (jawab al-qasam), and the scholars differed about it in several ways.

The first: what al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) mentioned, that the answer to the oath is His saying, ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾, with the lam (of emphasis) understood within it, as in His saying: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams 91:1] ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams 91:9], meaning: "Indeed he has succeeded." He said: "If you wish, it is on the basis of inversion (al-taqdim), as if it were said: 'Destroyed were the people of the trench, and by the sky with its constellations.'"

The second: what al-Zajjaj mentioned, that the answer to the oath is: ﴿Indeed the seizing of your Lord is severe﴾ [al-Buruj 85:12]. This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah.

The third: that the answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted﴾ [al-Buruj 85:10], and so on. It is like your saying: "By God, indeed Zayd is standing." Except that between the oath and its answer there intervenes His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted﴾.

The fourth: what a group of the earlier scholars mentioned, that the answer to the oath is omitted. This is the choice of the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). However, the earlier scholars said that the omitted matter is that the affair is true regarding the recompense for deeds. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The answer to the oath is what His saying ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾ indicates, as if it were said: 'He swore by these things that the disbelievers of Quraysh are cursed just as the people of the trench were cursed.' This is because the surah came to strengthen the believers and make them patient against the harm of the people of Makkah, and to remind them of what befell those who came before them of torment for faith, so that they might take them as examples, bear patiently the harm of their people, and know that the disbelievers of Makkah are in the sight of God in the same position as those in the earlier nations who burned the people of faith with fire. They deserve to be said of: 'Quraysh has been destroyed,' just as: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench.﴾"

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: they mentioned the story of the people of the trench in various accounts, and we will mention three of them.

The first: there was a sorcerer for one of the kings. When he grew old, a boy was attached to him to teach him sorcery. On the boy's path was a monk, and the boy's heart inclined toward that monk. Then one day the boy saw on his path a serpent that had blocked the people. He took a stone and said: "O God, if the monk is more beloved to You than the sorcerer, then strengthen me to kill it by throwing the stone at it." Then he threw and killed it. This became the cause of the boy's turning away from sorcery and his occupation with the monk's way. Then he came to the point where he would heal the blind from birth and the leper, and cure other illnesses. It happened that a companion of the king went blind, and the boy healed him. When the king saw him, he said: "Who restored your sight?" He said: "My Lord." The king became angry and tortured him, and he pointed to the boy. The king tortured the boy, and he pointed to the monk. The monk was brought and was ordered to abandon his religion, but the monk did not accept his words, so he was sawn in two with a saw. Then they brought the boy to a mountain to throw him from its peak, but he prayed to God, and the mountain shook beneath the people, so they perished and he was saved. Then they took him to a ship and sailed with him in order to drown him, but he prayed to God, and the ship capsized with them, so they drowned and he was saved. He said to the king: "You will not kill me until you gather the people in an open ground, crucify me on a trunk, take an arrow from my quiver, and say: 'In the name of God, the Lord of the boy,' then shoot me with it." So he shot him, and it struck his temple. He placed his hand upon it and died. The people said: "We believe in the Lord of the boy." It was said to the king: "What you were fearing has befallen you." So he ordered trenches to be dug at the mouths of the lanes, and fires were kindled in them. Whoever did not return [from faith] from among them, he threw into them. Then there came a woman with a child, and she hesitated to fall into it. The child said: "O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth." So she endured that.

The second narration: it was narrated from Ali, peace be upon him, that when they differed regarding the rulings concerning the Magians, he said: "They are People of the Book," [Page 108] and they were adhering to their Book. Wine had been made lawful to them, and one of their kings drank it, became intoxicated, and had relations with his sister. When he sobered up, he regretted it and sought a way out. His sister said to him: "The way out is that you address the people and say: 'God the Exalted has made lawful the marrying of sisters,' and then you address them after that and say: 'After that, He has forbidden it.'" He addressed them, but they did not accept this from him. She said to him: "Lash them with the whip." They did not accept it. She said: "Strike them with the sword." They did not accept it. So she ordered him to [dig] the trenches and kindle the fires, and to cast into them whoever came [to the trenches]. These are the ones God intended by His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench.﴾

The third narration: a man from among those who were upon the religion of Jesus came to Najran, and he invited them, and they responded to him. Dhu Nuwas the Jew came to them with troops from Himyar and gave them the choice between the fire and Judaism, but they refused. So he burned of them twelve thousand in the trenches; it was also said seventy thousand. It is mentioned that the length of the trench was forty cubits and its width twelve cubits.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever the people of the trench were mentioned, he would seek refuge in God from the severity of affliction.

If it is said: "The contradiction among these narrations indicates that they are false," we say: there is no contradiction. It was said that this happened in three regions, three times: once in Yemen, once in Iraq, and once in Syria. The word "al-ukhdud" (trench), although singular, is intended in the plural sense, and this is common in the Qur'an. Al-Qaffal said: "They mentioned in the story of the people of the trench varying narrations, and none of them is sound, except that they agree that they were a group of believers who opposed their people, or a disbelieving king who was ruling over them, and he threw them into a trench and dug it for them." Then he said: "I think that this event was well known among Quraysh, so God mentioned it to the companions of His Messenger as a reminder to them of what is required of them of patience in their religion and enduring its hardships. The idolaters of Quraysh were harming the believers, as the reports are well known regarding their exaggeration in harming Ammar and Bilal."

The second issue: al-ukhdud (the trench) is a cleft in the earth dug lengthwise. Its plural is al-akhadid, and its verbal root is al-khadd, which is a cleft. It is said: "He cleft the earth, a cleaving (khadd), and his flesh became cracked (takhaddada) when it became streaks like cracks."

The third issue: the people of the trench may refer to the killers, or it may refer to the killed. The well-known narration is that the killed were the believers. It is also narrated that the killed were the tyrants, because when they threw the believers into the fire, the fire turned back upon the disbelievers and burned them, and God saved the believers from it unharmed. To this view went al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Waqidi, and they interpreted His saying: ﴿For them is the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of burning﴾ [al-Buruj 85:10] as meaning: for them is the punishment of Hell in the Hereafter, and for them is the punishment of burning in this world.

Having understood this introduction, we say: they mentioned in the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾ three aspects, because we either interpret the people of the trench as the killers or as the killed.

As for the first aspect, there are two explanations:

One: that this is an invocation against them, meaning: "May the people of the trench be cursed." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Destroyed is man, how ungrateful he is﴾ [Abasa 80:17], and ﴿Destroyed are the liars﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:10].

The second: that the meaning is that those killers were destroyed by the fire, as we have mentioned: when the tyrants wanted to kill the believers by fire, the fire turned back upon them and destroyed them. As for when we interpret the people of the trench as the killed, the meaning is that those believers were killed by burning with fire, and in that case it is a report, not an invocation.

The fourth issue: it has been read as quttila with the doubled letter (qutthila).

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The fire fueled with wood﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: fire is only great when there is something that burns in it, whether wood or other fuel. So al-wuqud (fuel) is the name of that thing, as in His saying: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:6]. In ﴿fueled with wood﴾ there is a magnification of the matter of the great quantity of wood that was in that trench.

The second issue: Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: "This is a badal al-ishtimal (comprehensive apposition), like your saying: 'Zayd was stripped of his garment,' for the trench encompasses the fire."

The third issue: al-wuqud has been read with a ḍammah (al-wuqud, with ḍammah on the waw), which is the fuel itself.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when they sat beside it﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: the agent in "idh" (when) is "qutila" (destroyed). The meaning is: they were cursed at the time when they were sitting beside the trench, torturing the believers.

The second issue: there is a difficulty in the verse, which is that the pronoun in "hum" (they) refers to the people of the trench, since that is the nearest of the things mentioned, and the pronoun in "'alayha" (beside it) refers to the fire. This implies that the people of the trench were sitting upon the fire, and it is known that the matter was not like that.

The answer is from several aspects:

One: the pronoun in "hum" refers to the people of the trench, but what is meant here by the people of the trench are the killed, not the killers. So the meaning is: "when the believers were sitting upon the fire, burning, cast down upon the fire."

Two: the pronoun in "'alayha" may be taken as referring to the edge of the fire, its brink, and the places where it is possible to sit. The word "'ala" (upon) indicates this; you say "I passed by 'alayha," meaning: passing above a place close to it. So the ones who were doing the act were sitting by it, and they would present the believers before the fire: whoever was abandoning his religion, they left him; and whoever was patient in his religion, they cast him into the fire.

Three: suppose we grant that the pronoun in "hum" refers to the people of the trench in the sense of the killers, and the pronoun in "'alayha" refers to the fire. Why could it not be said that those killers were sitting upon the fire? For we have shown that when they cast the believers into the fire, the fire rose up toward them, and they perished by the very thing they had done with their own hands to destroy others. So the verse indicates that in that state they were also cursed, and the meaning is that they lost both this world and the Hereafter.

Four: that "'ala" is in the sense of "'inda" (with/at), as it was said regarding His saying: ﴿And they have a sin against me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:14], meaning: "with me."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they were witnesses to what they were doing to the believers﴾, know that His saying "shuhud" (witnesses) may mean presence, and it may mean witnesses by whose testimony a claim is established. As for the first aspect, the meaning is that those tyrant killers were present at that act, watching it. The purpose of mentioning this is one of three matters: either to describe them with hardness of heart, since they were present and watching when the torment by fire was taking place; or to describe them with earnestness in confirming their disbelief and falsehood, since they attended those dreadful places and horrifying deeds; or to describe those believers who were killed with earnestness in their religion and persistence upon their truth, for the disbelievers were only present in that place hoping that when these believers saw them, they would be awed by their presence and ashamed to oppose them. Yet those believers did not turn to them, and remained steadfast upon their true religion.

If you say: "If the meaning of 'shuhud' is this, then it should have been said: 'and they were witnesses to what they did' (li-ma yaf'aluna) rather than 'upon what they were doing' ('ala ma yaf'aluna)?" We say: He used the word "'ala" in the sense that they were upon the ugliness of their act against these believers, namely burning them with fire, while they were present and watching those ugly deeds.

As for the second possibility, that "shuhud" means the testimony by which a claim is established, there are several aspects:

[Page 110]

First: they were made witnesses, testifying to one another before the king that none of them had neglected what he was commanded to do and entrusted with regarding the torment.

Second: they are witnesses over what they did to the believers, rendering their testimony on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur 24:24].

Third: these disbelievers were watching what they did to the believers by burning them with fire, such that if it had been done by others, they would have been witnesses to it. Yet despite this, compassion did not take hold of them, nor did any inclination or pity arise in their hearts.

Then they brought the boy to a mountain to throw him from its peak, but he prayed to God, and the mountain shook beneath the people, so they perished and he was saved. Then they took him to a ship and sailed with him in order to drown him, but he prayed to God, and the ship capsized with them, so they drowned and he was saved. He said to the king: "You will not kill me until you gather the people in an open ground, crucify me on a trunk, take an arrow from my quiver, and say: 'In the name of God, the Lord of the boy,' then shoot me with it." So he shot him, and it struck his temple. He placed his hand upon it and died. The people said: "We believe in the Lord of the boy." It was said to the king: "What you were fearing has befallen you." So he ordered trenches to be dug at the mouths of the lanes, and fires were kindled in them. Whoever did not return [from faith] from among them, he threw into them. Then there came a woman with a child, and she hesitated to fall into it. The child said: "O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth." So she endured that.

The second narration: it was narrated from Ali, peace be upon him, that when they differed regarding the rulings concerning the Magians, he said: "They are People of the Book," [Page 108] and they were adhering to their Book. Wine had been made lawful to them, and one of their kings drank it, became intoxicated, and had relations with his sister. When he sobered up, he regretted it and sought a way out. His sister said to him: "The way out is that you address the people and say: 'God the Exalted has made lawful the marrying of sisters,' and then you address them after that and say: 'After that, He has forbidden it.'" He addressed them, but they did not accept this from him. She said to him: "Lash them with the whip." They did not accept it. She said: "Strike them with the sword." They did not accept it. So she ordered him to [dig] the trenches and kindle the fires, and to cast into them whoever came [to the trenches]. These are the ones God intended by His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench.﴾

The third narration: a man from among those who were upon the religion of Jesus came to Najran, and he invited them, and they responded to him. Dhu Nuwas the Jew came to them with troops from Himyar and gave them the choice between the fire and Judaism, but they refused. So he burned of them twelve thousand in the trenches; it was also said seventy thousand. It is mentioned that the length of the trench was forty cubits and its width twelve cubits.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever the people of the trench were mentioned, he would seek refuge in God from the severity of affliction.

If it is said: "The contradiction among these narrations indicates that they are false," we say: there is no contradiction. It was said that this happened in three regions, three times: once in Yemen, once in Iraq, and once in Syria. The word "al-ukhdud" (trench), although singular, is intended in the plural sense, and this is common in the Qur'an. Al-Qaffal said: "They mentioned in the story of the people of the trench varying narrations, and none of them is sound, except that they agree that they were a group of believers who opposed their people, or a disbelieving king who was ruling over them, and he threw them into a trench and dug it for them." Then he said: "I think that this event was well known among Quraysh, so God mentioned it to the companions of His Messenger as a reminder to them of what is required of them of patience in their religion and enduring its hardships. The idolaters of Quraysh were harming the believers, as the reports are well known regarding their exaggeration in harming Ammar and Bilal."

The second issue: al-ukhdud (the trench) is a cleft in the earth dug lengthwise. Its plural is al-akhadid, and its verbal root is al-khadd, which is a cleft. It is said: "He cleft the earth, a cleaving (khadd), and his flesh became cracked (takhaddada) when it became streaks like cracks."

The third issue: the people of the trench may refer to the killers, or it may refer to the killed. The well-known narration is that the killed were the believers. It is also narrated that the killed were the tyrants, because when they threw the believers into the fire, the fire turned back upon the disbelievers and burned them, and God saved the believers from it unharmed. To this view went al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Waqidi, and they interpreted His saying: ﴿For them is the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of burning﴾ [al-Buruj 85:10] as meaning: for them is the punishment of Hell in the Hereafter, and for them is the punishment of burning in this world.

Having understood this introduction, we say: they mentioned in the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾ three aspects, because we either interpret the people of the trench as the killers or as the killed.

As for the first aspect, there are two explanations:

One: that this is an invocation against them, meaning: "May the people of the trench be cursed." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Destroyed is man, how ungrateful he is﴾ [Abasa 80:17], and ﴿Destroyed are the liars﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:10].

The second: that the meaning is that those killers were destroyed by the fire, as we have mentioned: when the tyrants wanted to kill the believers by fire, the fire turned back upon them and destroyed them. As for when we interpret the people of the trench as the killed, the meaning is that those believers were killed by burning with fire, and in that case it is a report, not an invocation.

The fourth issue: it has been read as quttila with the doubled letter (qutthila).

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The fire fueled with wood﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: fire is only great when there is something that burns in it, whether wood or other fuel. So al-wuqud (fuel) is the name of that thing, as in His saying: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim 66:6]. In ﴿fueled with wood﴾ there is a magnification of the matter of the great quantity of wood that was in that trench.

The second issue: Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: "This is a badal al-ishtimal (comprehensive apposition), like your saying: 'Zayd was stripped of his garment,' for the trench encompasses the fire."

The third issue: al-wuqud has been read with a ḍammah (al-wuqud, with ḍammah on the waw), which is the fuel itself.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when they sat beside it﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: the agent in "idh" (when) is "qutila" (destroyed). The meaning is: they were cursed at the time when they were sitting beside the trench, torturing the believers.

The second issue: there is a difficulty in the verse, which is that the pronoun in "hum" (they) refers to the people of the trench, since that is the nearest of the things mentioned, and the pronoun in "'alayha" (beside it) refers to the fire. This implies that the people of the trench were sitting upon the fire, and it is known that the matter was not like that.

The answer is from several aspects:

One: the pronoun in "hum" refers to the people of the trench, but what is meant here by the people of the trench are the killed, not the killers. So the meaning is: "when the believers were sitting upon the fire, burning, cast down upon the fire."

Two: the pronoun in "'alayha" may be taken as referring to the edge of the fire, its brink, and the places where it is possible to sit. The word "'ala" (upon) indicates this; you say "I passed by 'alayha," meaning: passing above a place close to it. So the ones who were doing the act were sitting by it, and they would present the believers before the fire: whoever was abandoning his religion, they left him; and whoever was patient in his religion, they cast him into the fire.

Three: suppose we grant that the pronoun in "hum" refers to the people of the trench in the sense of the killers, and the pronoun in "'alayha" refers to the fire. Why could it not be said that those killers were sitting upon the fire? For we have shown that when they cast the believers into the fire, the fire rose up toward them, and they perished by the very thing they had done with their own hands to destroy others. So the verse indicates that in that state they were also cursed, and the meaning is that they lost both this world and the Hereafter.

Four: that "'ala" is in the sense of "'inda" (with/at), as it was said regarding His saying: ﴿And they have a sin against me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:14], meaning: "with me."

As for the first aspect, the meaning is that those tyrant killers were present at that act, watching it. The purpose of mentioning this is one of three matters: either to describe them with hardness of heart, since they were present and watching when the torment by fire was taking place; or to describe them with earnestness in confirming their disbelief and falsehood, since they attended those dreadful places and horrifying deeds; or to describe those believers who were killed with earnestness in their religion and persistence upon their truth, for the disbelievers were only present in that place hoping that when these believers saw them, they would be awed by their presence and ashamed to oppose them. Yet those believers did not turn to them, and remained steadfast upon their true religion.

If you say: "If the meaning of 'shuhud' is this, then it should have been said: 'and they were witnesses to what they did' (li-ma yaf'aluna) rather than 'upon what they were doing' ('ala ma yaf'aluna)?" We say: He used the word "'ala" in the sense that they were upon the ugliness of their act against these believers, namely burning them with fire, while they were present and watching those ugly deeds.

As for the second possibility, that "shuhud" means the testimony by which a claim is established, there are several aspects:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 85, verse 10:

Page 111

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who put the believing men and believing women to trial and then do not repent will have the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of the People of the Ditch, He followed it with what branches out from it of the rulings on reward and punishment, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who put the believing men﴾ and here are some issues:

The first issue: It is possible that what is meant by it is only the People of the Ditch, and it is possible that what is meant is everyone who did that, and this is preferable, because the wording is general and the ruling is general, so restricting it is abandoning the apparent meaning without evidence.

The second issue: The root of fitnah (trial, a testing or tormenting) is testing and examination, because those disbelievers tested those believers, presented them to the fire and burned them. Some exegetes said that fitnah is burning with fire. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: ﴿put [them] to trial﴾ means they burned them with fire. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "fatantu al-shay'" meaning "I burned the thing," and al-fatn are black stones as if they were burnt, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿on the Day when they will be tried over the Fire﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13].

The third issue: His saying, ﴿and then do not repent﴾ indicates that if they had repented, they would have been exempt from this threat, and this indicates with certainty that Allah, exalted is He, accepts repentance, and it indicates that the repentance of one who kills intentionally is accepted, contrary to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿then for them is the punishment of Hell, and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: that both punishments occur in the Hereafter, except that the punishment of Hell is the punishment resulting from their disbelief, and the punishment of the Burning is the punishment added to the punishment of disbelief because they burned the believers. So it is possible that the first punishment is the punishment of cold and the second is the punishment of burning, and it is possible that the first is the punishment of burning and the additional one beyond burning is also burning, except that the first punishment is, as it were, excluded from being called burning in comparison to the second, because the second has combined two kinds of burning, so it became very complete, and the first became weak, therefore it was not called burning.

The second opinion: that His saying, ﴿then for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, and ﴿and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ refers to what we mentioned, that those disbelievers were overtaken by the fire of the Ditch and were burned by it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 85, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great attainment.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the threat against the criminals, He mentioned the promise to the believers, which is clear. In it there are two issues:

The first issue: He said ﴿That is the attainment﴾ and did not say "Those are the attainment," for a subtle reason. His saying "that" (dhalika) refers to Allah's report of the existence of these gardens, while His saying "those" (tilka) refers to the gardens themselves. Allah's report about this indicates His being pleased, and "the great attainment" is the pleasure of Allah, not merely the obtaining of Paradise.

Page 112

The second issue: The story of the People of the Trench, and especially this verse, indicates that one who is compelled to disbelief by the threat of great destruction is better off enduring what he is feared for, and that uttering the word of disbelief is like a concession in that matter. "Al-Hasan narrated that Musaylimah seized two men from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). He said to one of them: 'Do you testify that I am the Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes,' so he let him go. He said the same to the other, and he said: 'No, rather you are a liar,' so he killed him. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: 'As for the one who was let go, he took the concession, so there is no blame on him. As for the one who was killed, he took the higher virtue, so congratulations to him.'"

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 85, verses 12–16:**

God's words: ﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats.﴾ ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving.﴾ ﴿Lord of the Throne, the Glorious.﴾ ﴿Doer of whatever He intends.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, first mentioned the threat against those who tormented the believing men and women, and then mentioned the promise to those who believed and did righteous deeds, He followed that promise and threat with emphasis. For the emphasis of the threat He said: ﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe.﴾ *Al-batsh* is seizing with violence. When it is described as severe, it is intensified and grows greater. A parallel is ﴿Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe﴾ [Hud: 102]. Furthermore, this One who is capable does not delay out of neglect, but because He is wise, either by the decree of His will or by the decree of what is good. The postponement of this matter until the Day of Resurrection is for this reason. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats.﴾ That is, He creates His creation, then causes them to perish, then restores them alive so that He may recompense them on the Resurrection. So that delay is for this cause, not out of neglect. Ibn Abbas said: "The people of Hell will be consumed by the Fire until they become charcoal, then He will restore them as a new creation." That is what is meant by His words: ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats.﴾

Then, for the emphasis of the promise, He said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving.﴾ Thus He mentioned five of the attributes of His majesty and greatness.

The first is *al-Ghafur* (the Forgiving). The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: He is the Forgiving toward whoever repents. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: He is Forgiving absolutely, toward whoever repents and toward whoever does not repent, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 48]. Also, forgiving the penitent is obligatory, and performing an obligation does not merit praise, whereas this verse is mentioned in the context of praise.

The second is *al-Wadud* (the Loving), and concerning it there are several views.

One: it means *al-Muhibb* (the One who loves). This is the view of most exegetes, and it agrees with rational proofs, for good is necessary in its essence and evil is accidental, and evil must be less than good, so what prevails must be good, and therefore He is loved in His essence.

Two: al-Kalbi said: *al-Wadud* is the One who shows affection toward His friends through forgiveness and reward. The first view is the correct one.

Three: al-Azhari said: some of the lexicographers said it is permissible that *wadud* is *fa'ul* in the sense of *maf'ul*, like *rakub* and *halub*, and its meaning is that His righteous servants love Him and affection for Him, because they have recognized His perfection in His essence, attributes and actions. He said: both attributes are praise, because when He, great is His remembrance, loves His obedient servants, that is His grace; and when His knowing servants love Him, that is because of the generous goodness that is established for them.

Four: al-Qaffal said: it has been said that *al-Wadud* may mean *al-Halim* (the Forbearing), from the saying "a *wadud* beast," which means one that is obedient to the rein: however you bend it, it bends. Qutrub recited:

"I have prepared for war a swift mare, obedient to the rein, bold, and gentle."

[Page 113]

The third is *dhu al-Arsh* (Lord of the Throne). Al-Qaffal said: *Dhu al-Arsh* means *dhu al-mulk wa al-sultan* (possessor of dominion and authority), as one says "so-and-so is on the throne of his kingdom" even if he is not on a throne, and as one says "the throne of so-and-so has collapsed" when his authority has gone. This meaning is agreed upon as correct. It is also possible that the intended meaning of *al-arsh* is a throne, and that He, exalted is His majesty, created a throne in His heaven of utmost greatness and majesty, such that no one knows its greatness except Him and whomever He informs of it.

The fourth is *al-Majid* (the Glorious), and concerning it there are two readings.

One: the nominative (*raf'*), so that it is an attribute of Allah, glorified is He. This is the choice of most readers and exegetes, because glory belongs to attributes of exaltedness and majesty, and this befits none but Allah, glorified is He. Separation and interjection between the attribute and the described in this type of construction is not impermissible.

The second reading: the genitive (*khafd*), which is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Then the attribute is of the Throne. These said: the Qur'an indicates that it is permissible to describe other than Allah as *majid*, where He said: ﴿Rather, it is a Glorious Qur'an﴾, and we see that Allah described the Throne as *karim* (noble), so it is not far-fetched that He also describes it as *majid*. Then they said: the glory of Allah is His greatness according to the necessity of His essential existence and the perfection of power, wisdom and knowledge; while the greatness of the Throne is its height in direction, the greatness of its magnitude, and the beauty of its form and composition, for it has been said: the Throne is the most beautifully composed and formed of bodies.

The fifth is that He is *fa'al li-ma yurid* (Doer of whatever He intends), and concerning it there are several issues.

Issue one: *fa'al* is the predicate of an omitted subject.

Issue two: Some grammarians said: "the Forgiving, the Loving" are two predicates of one subject. This is weak, because what is intended by ascribing to the subject either is their combined whole, or each one of them individually. If it is the first, the predicate is one for the other two; and if it is the second, the statement becomes two propositions, not one proposition before two propositions.

Issue three: Our companions used this verse in the question of the creation of acts. They said: there is no doubt that He, exalted is He, wills faith, so it must be that He is the doer of faith according to the implication of this verse; and if He is the doer of faith, it must be that He is the doer of disbelief, because no one holds a distinction. Al-Qadi said: one cannot use this to prove that what Allah, exalted is He, wills of the obedience of creatures must occur, because His words, ﴿Doer of whatever He intends﴾, only encompass what, if it occurs, is His act, not what, if it occurs, is not an act of His. These are al-Qadi's words, and their weakness is not hidden.

Issue four: Our companions used this verse to show that Allah, exalted is He, is not obligated to any of the accountable beings in anything at all. This is weak, because the verse indicates that He does what He wills, so why do you say that He wills not to give the reward?

Issue five: Al-Qaffal said: *fa'al li-ma yurid* means according to what He sees; no objector objects to Him and no conqueror overcomes Him. He admits His allies to Paradise, and no one prevents Him from doing so; He admits His enemies to the Fire, and no helper supports them against Him; He gives the disobedient respite as He wills until He recompenses them, and He hastens the punishment of some of them when He wills, and He punishes whomever He wills of them in this world and in the Hereafter. He does these things and others besides, whatever He wills.

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the condition of the People of the Trench in their harming of the believers by the disbelievers, He explained that those before them were likewise. Thamud were in the lands of the Arabs, and their story is well known among them. So He mentioned Pharaoh from the later ones and Thamud from the earlier ones. The purpose is to make clear that the condition of the believers with the disbelievers is continuous in this manner in all times, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve persist in denial.﴾ When He had consoled the heart of the Messenger, peace be upon him, by relating the conditions of the earlier peoples in this matter, He then consoled him from another aspect, which is His saying: ﴿and Allah encompasses them from behind.﴾ On this there are several views:
